newsitem.title: USA: S.Africa prospects rely on medium-term program - S&P.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa prospects rely on medium-term program - S&P.

text.p: The key to South Africa's credit improvement lies with its medium-term fiscal program and improving investor confidence in the country's economic prospects, Standard and Poor's said Thursday.

Guido Cipriani, director of sovereign ratings at S&P, said main challenges to raising the country's BB-plus long-term foreign currency rating rested with further implementation of the government's economic plan.
"I would certainly highlight the fiscal consolidation and asset restructuring program of the government," Cipriani said on a teleconference here.
He said that an IMF loan might aid short-term confidence, but the most important elements to S&P's rating considerations lay in the government's medium-term policy.

"The most important issue for us is whether the policies are right and whether the implementation prospects are reasonable," Cipriani said. "We're suggesting that the answer to both of those questions is yes."
Last week, S&P said that its outlook remained positive on South Africa's foreign exchange rating, as well as its BBB-plus local currency rating.

Cipriani said the rand seemed to be "quite vulnerable," given the country's current account deficit, relatively low capital inflows and low reserves, but he said the government had articulated a clear strategy to address the problem.
"The prospects for the rand going forward will revolve around the extent to which investors increasingly believe that the government can deliver on the program," Cipriani said.

He noted that most observers seemed to think that the rand's slump since February had been excessive, and the real effective exchange rate should stabilize near-term should government policies be implemented.
The S&P rating does not depend on the presence of President Nelson Mandela, as the credit standing is supported by increasing political stability in the country, Cipriani said.
"There is a great resilience in the political story in South Africa," he said.
